item.title: Dean Saranillio
item.dc:creator: cssweb
item.content:encoded:
Dean Saranillio

Associate Professor, Graduate Chair
Office: Saunders 613
Telephone: 1 (808) 956-3688
Email: dsaranil@hawaii.edu

Browse My Publications:

Background

I grew up in the working-class town of Kahului on the island of Maui. In 1895, my great-grandparents migrated from Nigata and Fukushima, Japan. In 1919, my great-grandparents on my father's side settled from Cebu in the Philippines. While shaped by my family's histories on the plantations, it wasn't until I was an undergraduate student at UH that I began thinking about questions of US imperialism. Haunani-Kay Trask's mentorship radically transformed my sense of the world and the political possibilities for Hawai'i's future. Her courses gave me the language to describe the interlocking systems of settler colonialism, labor, racial capitalism, militarism, and various forms of resistance that shape our communities. I continued my education at UCLA and the University of Michigan. I was faculty at the University of California, Riverside and New York University where I received tenure.

Education

  • PhD, American Culture, University of Michigan, 2009
  • MA, Asian American Studies, University of California, Los Angeles, 2003
  • BA, Ethnic Studies, University of Hawai'i at Mānoa, 2001

Courses

  • POLS 271: Race and Politics
  • POLS 301: Hawai'i Politics
  • POLS 303: (Alpha) Topics in Hawai'i Politics
  • POLS 379: Power and America
  • POLS 385: American Politics
  • POLS 686: Politics of Hawai'i
  • POLS 600: Scope and Methods

Research

As a scholar of race and empire informed by Indigenous Studies, my research examines how settler colonialism eliminates alternatives to itself. My scholarship, teaching, and activism traces the plurality of possibilities that might emerge when non-Native residents work in place-based affinity with Native foodways, economies, and movements. My recent work shows how capitalism is continually birthed and rebirthed through the death of non-human relations and that this particular mode of production has evolved to set the current environmental conditions of climate crisis.

item.title: Debbie Samaniego
item.dc:creator: cssweb
item.content:encoded:
Debbie Samaniego

Assistant Professor
Office: Saunders 614
Telephone: 1 (808) 956-7180
Email: dsamanie@hawaii.edu

Browse My Publications:

Background

I am a first-generation Latina who grew up in California and Utah. I completed my BA in Political Science at Westminster College in Salt Lake City. After receiving a Marshall Scholarship, I went on to pursue my graduate studies in the United Kingdom. I received a MA in International Relations from Queen Mary University of London in 2018 and my PhD in International Relations from the University of Sussex in 2022. My family's background as working-class migrants in the US has significantly shaped my research and political commitments to social justice and education. I continuously strive to be a critical and compassionate educator.

Education

  • PhD, International Relations, University of Sussex, 2022
  • MA, International Relations, Queen Mary University of London, 2018
  • BA, Political Science, Westminster College, 2017

Courses

  • POLS 150: Introduction to Global Politics
  • POLS 600: Scopes and Methods of Political Science

Research

My research draws on a range of critical approaches, most prominently decolonial and settler colonial studies to examine migration politics within the modern international order. I am currently working on a book manuscript titled Rethinking Migration through the Colonial Question which argues that the US is not experiencing a migration crisis at its southern border, but rather a colonial crisis.

Broadly, I am working on three strands of research. First, I examine the coloniality of global migration governance, including the externalization and militarization of borders. Second, I analyse the historical continuity of racialized migrant labor regimes in the US, UK, and EU. Third, I study colonial/imperial projects in Latin America and their relationship to displacement and forced migration.

item.title: Felix Mantz
item.dc:creator: cssweb
item.content:encoded:
Felix Mantz

Assistant Professor
Office: Saunders 611
Telephone: 1 (808) 956-8357
Email: fmantz@hawaii.edu

Browse My Publications:

Background

I grew up in different parts of Germany before starting my undergraduate studies in the US. It was then that my interest in politics was ignited as I learned to study the modern international order and its global political economy from Third World, anti-colonial, and Indigenous perspectives. Concerned with the convergence of unprecedented crises afflicting this order as well as the different forms of injustice and violence they produce, I went on to complete my graduate studies at King's College London and Queen Mary University of London. Prior to joining UH, I held research and teaching positions at SOAS University of London, the Free University of Brighton, and California State University San Marcos.

Education

  • PhD, Political Science, Queen Mary University of London, 2023
  • MRes, International Relations, Queen Mary University of London, 2019
  • MA, International Political Economy, King's College London, 2018
  • BA, Critical Global Studies, Westminster University, 2017

Courses

  • POLS 110: Introduction to Political Science
  • POLS 305: Global Politics/ Comparative
  • POLS 380: Environmental Law and Politics
  • POLS 600: Scope and Methods of Political Science
  • POLS 630: International Relations
  • POLS 730: Seminar in International Relations

Research

My research is interdisciplinary, spanning across International Political Economy, Environmental Politics, Anti/Decolonial Studies, and Development Studies. I specifically work on the ways in which the global political economy, planetary environmental crises, and colonial structures of power are entangled. Drawing on a range of critical theories, especially anti/decolonial, anti-capitalist, anarchist, and Indigenous thought, I am especially interested in questions of land, socio-ecological liberation, autonomy, food systems, and extractivism. My teaching and research are based on a commitment to challenge oppressive systems of power and, as the Zapatistas would put it, recover, (re)build, and defend a world in which many worlds fit. Most of my work has a regional focus on East Africa and Mesoamerica.

Community Engagement

Knowledge, learning, and education are not property or commodities to be owned, sold, or leveraged to reproduce social hierarchies. They are relations and activities that are generated by society as a whole and thus belong to all. Between 2021 and 2023, I have worked with the Free University of Brighton (UK), a moneyless, autonomous learning space that seeks to make higher education free and accessible to everyone. Besides my academic publications, I have also written a series of public-facing articles which can be found, among others, in Global Social Theory, Discover Society, and E-International Relations (E-IR). I was previously Commissioning Editor for E-IR.
